title: Tongues and colors
hook: the diversity of your languages and colors is among His signs (30:22)

segments.voice: Yesterday, mawadda and rahma, and your line was love and mercy between. Who did you do the small thing for, and how did they take it? Day five hundred thirty-two, the end of the week.

Stand in the courtyard of the Great Mosque in Mecca at any hour, and listen. Indonesian, Urdu, Turkish, Hausa, Bosnian, Malay, Bengali, Somali, French, English, Arabic in a dozen accents. Faces of every shade, from every continent, walking the same circle, many in the same white cloth. Some pilgrims come home talking less about the buildings than about the crowd. The verse right after yesterday's has a word for what they saw.

Pickthall: "And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours. Lo! herein indeed are portents for men of knowledge." Look at the company the verse keeps. The heavens, the earth, and then, in the same breath, the fact that people speak differently and look different. Human variety is put on the same shelf as the sky. Not a problem to be solved, and not a ranking. A sign, an aya, the same word used for a verse of the Qur'an. And who is meant to read this sign? Men of knowledge, in Pickthall's English; in Arabic, al-'alimin, those who know. As if the more you learn about people, the more there is to see. The Qur'an says something close in Surah Al-Hujurat: We made you nations and tribes so that you might know one another, and the noblest of you with God is the most mindful of Him. And in the sermon the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave at his farewell pilgrimage, reported in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, he said an Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, nor a light-skinned person over a dark-skinned one, nor the reverse, except by taqwa. His first community already looked like that: Bilal from Abyssinia, Salman from Persia, Suhayb, called the Roman. This week ran from Al-Qasas through Al-'Ankabut to Ar-Rum: al-amin, do good as good was done, faith is tested, al-'ankabut, within a few years, love and mercy between. And today, the widest one: difference is a sign.
screen: `LANGUAGES AND COLORS BESIDE THE SKY.` · `A SIGN FOR THOSE WHO KNOW.` · `NATIONS AND TRIBES, TO KNOW ONE ANOTHER.` · `NO ARAB OVER NON-ARAB, EXCEPT BY TAQWA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn a greeting in another language. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of someone you see often whose first language isn't yours. A neighbor, a colleague, the person who runs the corner shop, a classmate's parent. What language do they speak at home? Decide to learn how to say hello, or thank you, in it. Picture saying it to them, a little clumsily, and seeing their face change. If you pray, you can thank God for one person whose difference has taught you something. The bell holds the time.
Aya. A sign, the same word used for a verse of the Qur'an: what Ar-Rum calls the variety of human languages and colors, beside the heavens and the earth. Today's word.
Your line: difference is a sign. Today, use the greeting you learned, even if you get it a bit wrong. Day five hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims often cite 30:22, 49:13 and the Prophet's farewell sermon to teach that no language, people or color is above another, and that only taqwa distinguishes people before God.

fork.setup: you're on Hajj, surrounded by a crowd whose languages you don't speak. the verse calls this a sign. for whom?
options: for those who know: the more you learn, the more you see.
for nobody; it's just a crowd.
fork.reveal: 30:22: herein indeed are portents for those who know, al-'alimin.

original.note: Arabic: your tongues and your colors, from 30:22; alsina is literally tongues.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about diversity.
what it means: human variety is placed among God's signs, like the sky, to be read by people who learn.
what a scholar hears: ikhtilafu alsinatikum wa alwanikum, a sign for al-'alimin; read with 49:13's li-ta'arafu and the farewell sermon in Musnad Ahmad.
recall: the one forced into a corner

notes: Week-end day (526–532): the teach names the week's lines.
Pickthall 30:22 quoted from memory; confirm wording. The Arabic reading al-'alimin (with kasra, 'those who know') is the Hafs reading; some read al-'alamin ('the worlds'). Confirm how to present it.
Musnad Ahmad 23489 cited from memory; confirm number and the paraphrase.
Suhayb 'al-Rumi' was of Arab origin raised among the Byzantines; 'called the Roman' is accurate as a nickname. Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the week recap wrongly said the whole week came from 'the stories surah' (Al-Qasas); it ran across Al-Qasas, Al-'Ankabut and Ar-Rum, now said so; the hook's claim about what pilgrims 'often say' and 'didn't expect to be moved by' narrowed to 'some pilgrims'; 'thousands' in the fork removed.
